% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
% TITLE + CITATION  (masthead repeats in the page header)

\brieftitle{Losing a home in a wildfire costs more than just the rebuild}
\briefcitation{Lessons from ``The Distribution and Consequences of Natural Disasters: Evidence from U.S. Wildfire Victims'' by Patrick Baylis, Judson Boomhower, Jonathan Colmer, and John Voorheis, NBER Working Paper, 2026.}

\vspace{-2pt}

% override body font size for this document
\fontsize{10.5pt}{13.5pt}\selectfont

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
% BOTTOM LINE  (~40–50 words)
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
% GUIDANCE: Core claim = when a wildfire destroys a home, occupants don't
% just lose the structure — they lose income too, for years afterward.
% Headline number: cumulative income losses equal to 30% of pre-fire annual
% income (~$38,000), concentrated entirely among occupants of DESTROYED
% homes. Occupants of homes that survived the same fire, and people living
% just outside the perimeter, show no measurable income effect — so the
% loss tracks losing the home, not living through the fire. Causality here
% is comparatively clean (Grant) — state it plainly, minimal hedging needed.
\begin{bottomline}
{\fontsize{11pt}{15pt}\selectfont
New research studying nearly all wildfires in the past 25 years shows that \textbf{when a wildfire destroys a home, occupants don't just lose the structure — they lose income too, for years afterward.} 
}
\end{bottomline}

\vspace{6pt}

% BACKGROUND  (~120 words, 2 paragraphs)

\sectionhead{Background}
% GUIDANCE — Para 1 (set the scene, narrow to the study):
%   - Grant's suggested open: global natural-catastrophe losses ($320B in
%     2024, Munich Re) -> narrow to "the near-universe of catastrophic U.S.
%     wildfires" this paper studies (~150 fires, 2003-2022, matched to
%     individual damage assessments).
%   - Frame the three-part question (Grant's hourglass): who ends up living
%     in a fire's path and whose home actually burns; what happens to a
%     household's finances after a home is destroyed; how the neighborhood
%     itself changes during recovery.
%   - Wildfires are increasing — climate change, more building in fire-prone
%     areas, fuel buildup from past suppression (paper's Conclusion) — a
%     natural stakes-setting line per the meeting notes ("we need to think
%     about all of the decisions that go into policies around this issue").
% Para 2 (setting + data):
%   - Property-level damage assessments for those fires, linked to IRS tax
%     records and Census microdata — lets the study follow the SAME
%     individual before and after a fire, rather than only zip-code-level
%     averages that can't tell a burned-out household from an untouched
%     neighbor. This granularity is the paper's key methodological edge.
%   - Three groups compared: occupants of DESTROYED homes, occupants of
%     homes inside the fire perimeter that SURVIVED, and people living just
%     outside the perimeter.
% Wording (Grant, both notes): avoid "hazard" and "vulnerability" — use
% plain phrasing like "who lives in a fire's path" / "whose home actually
% burns."
% Candidate Background (page-1) figure: recreate Fig. 1 (map of destroyed/
% surviving/adjacent homes, 2020 Glass Fire) or Fig. 2 (pre-fire income
% distribution, destroyed vs. surviving occupants) to visualize who's
% exposed / whose home is lost. Grant: "room for doing some good framing
% here with the figures... be creative." Confirm exact point estimates with
% Grant before building the recreation script if reusing either — not all
% are disclosed directly in the paper text.
\noindent Global economic losses from natural catastrophes totaled \$320 billion in 2024. Though this number is striking, it masks that \textbf{the financial consequences of disasters are unevenly distributed across households.} To respond well to disasters, it's important to know who bears the losses, whether the damage to household finances goes beyond the cost of rebuilding, and what happens to a neighborhood as it recovers. This is especially true for areas prone to wildfires, which are increasing in frequency and severity.

\noindent \textbf{In a new working paper, Baylis et al. (2026) find that those whose homes were destroyed in a wildfire don't just lose the value of their house, they also lose a significant portion of their income for years afterward.} The researchers studied nearly all catastrophic wildfires in the United States from 2003 to 2022 and analyzed property damage alongside occupant demographics and income data. 

\vspace{6pt}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
% THE CHALLENGE  (~180–300 words) — the research-design story
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\sectionhead{The challenge}
% GUIDANCE — Grant: this causal story is comparatively straightforward
% (vs. the EPA compliance paper), so this section can be tighter/more direct.
%   - The obstacle: can't observe what would have happened to the SAME
%     people if their home hadn't burned. A simple before/after comparison
%     risks picking up ordinary local income trends, not the fire's effect.
%   - Comparing fire-zone residents to people elsewhere also confounds —
%     occupants of wildfire-affected homes are wealthier, more likely to be
%     white, and older than the U.S. population on average (Sec. 3.1),
%     simply because of WHERE wildfires tend to occur — that reflects who
%     lives in a fire's path, not the fire's effect.
%   - Their solution: compare occupants of destroyed homes to occupants of
%     homes in the SAME fire that survived, and to people living just
%     outside that fire's perimeter (0–10km / 10–25km rings) — tracking
%     each group's income in the years before and after.
%   - What makes it credible: pre-fire, all groups were on similar income
%     trajectories (no evidence of differential pre-trends) — so the
%     post-fire divergence can be attributed to the fire/home loss, not
%     pre-existing differences (meeting notes: "before, similar
%     trajectories between home losers, home survivors, and similar people
%     outside of fire perimeter").
% Optional color on why this is a large financial shock worth taking
% seriously (meeting notes): insurance often covers only 60–80% of a total
% loss, and a wave of local rebuilding demand can push reconstruction costs
% up further — destroyed-home occupants are absorbing a real financial hit
% before even counting the income losses this paper measures (paper
% footnote 8, re: insurance shortfalls in the 2021 Marshall Fire). Could
% live here or fold into Background instead.
\noindent \textbf{[State the core evaluation problem in one bold sentence a skimmer can catch.]} [Why seeing the counterfactual directly is impossible, so a stand-in comparison is needed.]

\noindent [The naive before/after comparison and why it misleads.]

\noindent [The next instinct — comparing against a different group — and the complication it introduces.]

\noindent [How the researchers got around it. \textbf{Bold the sentence naming the actual comparison they used.} Note what makes it fair.]

% FINDINGS  (~150 words + figure)
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
% GUIDANCE — headline finding (Grant's result 2, "the effects"):
%   - Occupants of DESTROYED homes see income fall for three years after
%     the fire, peaking around an 11% drop in year two, returning to the
%     comparison group's level by year four. Cumulative loss ≈ 30% of one
%     year's pre-fire income (~$38,000 on average).
%   - Critically: occupants of homes that SURVIVED the same fire, and
%     people living just outside the perimeter, show close to NO income
%     effect. The loss tracks whose home was actually destroyed — not
%     everyone who lived through the fire (meeting notes: "people don't
%     lose their house, they lose their earnings as well").
%   - The "why" is an open question the paper itself doesn't fully resolve
%     — worth naming as a limit/hook rather than speculating (e.g. time
%     spent managing rebuilding; reduced hours rather than job loss, since
%     employment rates barely move). Don't overclaim a mechanism the paper
%     doesn't test.
% Figure candidate: Fig. 4 Panel A ("The Effect of Wildfires on Income by
% Damage") — income trajectory for Destroyed vs. Survived vs. Adjacent,
% years -4 to +4 relative to the fire.
% Meeting-note tip: the event-study coefficients and the raw group-average
% trajectories "look pretty much the same" — a plainer raw-data line chart
% may read more intuitively to a general audience than a formal coefficient
% plot; worth trying both before committing.

\noindent [State the result, pointing the reader to the figure below. \textbf{Bold the headline finding.}]

\vspace{6pt}

\begin{center}
\begin{minipage}{0.75\linewidth}
\figtitle{The Wildfire's effect on income, year by year}{Source: Baylis, Boomhower, Colmer \& Voorheis (2026), Fig.\ 4a.}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{../data-viz/figures/fig1-income-by-damage.png}
\par\vspace{3pt}
{\color{faint}\fontsize{7.1pt}{9.5pt}\selectfont \textit{Note:} This figure shows the estimated effect of a wildfire on the incomes of people who lived inside its perimeter. One line follows occupants whose homes were destroyed; the other follows occupants of homes in the same fires that survived. Both are measured against similar people who lived just outside the perimeter, and both are set to zero in the year before the fire --- so a point below the line means that group had fallen behind those outside neighbors, and a point on the line means it had kept pace. The estimates account for occupants' characteristics and for anything that affected everyone caught in the same fire in the same year; the shaded bands show the range of uncertainty around each estimate. If losing a home, rather than living through a fire, is what costs people income, only the line for destroyed homes would fall after the fire. \par}
\end{minipage}
\end{center}
